name: Hydrogen peroxide gum rinse

angle.text: Diluted peroxide is swished as a gum antiseptic to calm gingivitis. Some trials support a benefit for gingivitis, though chlorhexidine is reported to be more effective.

summary: Dilute peroxide swished as a gum antiseptic; some trial support for gingivitis but chlorhexidine is reported more effective.
currentQuick:
A hydrogen peroxide rinse is a diluted solution swished in the mouth to reduce plaque and gum inflammation.
A review found it better than placebo for gingivitis but far less effective than chlorhexidine.
How it works: It acts as an antimicrobial and oxidising agent on oral bacteria and plaque.
Risks and caveats: Even 3% solutions can injure the eye; the FDA generally recognises peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial, not specifically for dental use.
deepLead:
A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution of hydrogen peroxide swished in the mouth as an antiseptic, used in the hope of reducing plaque and gum inflammation (gingivitis). Hydrogen peroxide is also found in many whitening products.
A review summarised on Wikipedia found a positive effect of dilute hydrogen peroxide over placebo for gingivitis and plaque, but concluded that chlorhexidine is far more effective. Gingivitis articles list hydrogen peroxide among antiseptic rinses used for prevention and home treatment.

name: Gum massage / Stillman technique

chain: Better plaque control and circulation claimed
angle.text: The Stillman technique and gum massage are discussed online as ways to improve gum health along the gumline. Little supporting evidence was found in the sources reviewed.

summary: A gumline brushing/gum-massage method; little evidence was found in the sources reviewed.
note: Hard pressure on gums is cautioned against in general guidance.
currentQuick:
The Stillman technique is a brushing method involving gentle gumline action, sometimes described as gum massage.
No trial evidence was found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Proponents say stimulating the gums improves circulation and plaque removal at the gumline.
Risks and caveats: General guidance cautions against pressing hard on teeth and gums.
deepLead:
The Stillman technique is a toothbrushing method named for a dental researcher, associated with gentle gum stimulation or massage alongside cleaning at the gumline. Gum massage is discussed in online circles as a way to improve gum health.
The pages consulted for this article do not describe the Stillman method or gum massage, so evidence is limited here. Wikipedia notes that technique advice from dental associations, companies and textbooks has been inconsistent, and that lay people clean at most about 40% of tooth margins at the gumline.

name: Dry mouth management (Biotene)

angle.text: Saliva substitutes such as Biotene are used to relieve dry mouth, which is tied to stale breath. They give short-term relief; no topical therapy has strong evidence.

summary: Saliva substitutes like Biotene give short-term dry-mouth relief; no topical therapy has strong evidence.
note: Acidic products below about pH 6.7 may risk root dentine.
currentQuick:
Dry mouth products such as Biotene are sprays, gels and rinses that coat the mouth to relieve dryness, used because lack of saliva raises risks of decay and bad breath.
Research summaries say none has strong evidence and benefits are short-term.
How it works: They lubricate and coat the mouth, imitating some of saliva's function; they do not restore salivary flow.
Risks and caveats: Products are generally low risk, though some acidic moisturisers may harm dentine, and sugar-containing ones may feed decay bacteria.
deepLead:
Dry mouth management refers to products and habits used to relieve xerostomia, the sensation of a dry mouth, including saliva substitutes in the form of sprays, gels, rinses and lozenges. Biotene is a widely sold brand of such products.
Dry mouth matters to dental appearance communities because lack of saliva, which buffers acid, is linked to rampant tooth decay, mouth soreness, candida infection and intraoral bad breath. Wikipedia reports that no topical therapy has strong evidence of effectiveness and that benefits are generally short-term.

name: Drinking water frequently

angle.text: Frequent water sipping is a common suggestion in breath-care guides for dry mouth and mouth odour. It is a low-cost habit, and trial evidence on its effect on odour was not found.

summary: Frequent sipping is commonly suggested for dry mouth; no trial evidence on odour was found.
currentQuick:
Drinking water frequently is a common suggestion for dry mouth and morning breath.
No specific trial of water for mouth odour was found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Water temporarily moistens the mouth and rinses debris; it does not restore saliva production.
Risks and caveats: Considered low risk; a 2017 paper noted bottled waters vary in pH.
deepLead:
Drinking water frequently is a habit recommended in many dry-mouth and breath-care guides as a way to relieve a dry mouth and reduce mouth odour. Wikipedia lists water among saliva substitutes but cites no specific trial for it.
Grokipedia advises sipping water every 15 to 30 minutes, noting that large amounts at once give only temporary relief. The Wikipedia halitosis article does not present water as a remedy, though it notes breath is worst on waking because of overnight dryness, and that a 2019 Cochrane review found no strong evidence on which interventions work best.

name: Quit smoking and vaping for breath

chain: Smoke odour and gum damage reduced
angle.text: Looksmaxxers quit smoking and vaping to lose smoke odour on the breath and protect the gums, as a low-cost grooming change. The gum-health link is well documented, while appearance-specific trials have not been done.

summary: Stopping tobacco and nicotine use to cut smoke odour and protect the gums; the gum-health link is well documented, appearance-specific trials are not.
note: Reference sources cover smoking and gum disease; vaping evidence was not found in them.
currentQuick:
Quitting smoking or vaping is discussed as a way to remove smoke odour from the breath and reduce damage to the gums.
Reference sources describe smoking as a major risk factor for gum disease, which is a recognised cause of bad breath, and say quitting improves gum health.
How it works: Smoking is described as impairing immune response and wound healing in the gums and contributing to periodontal disease, whose bacteria produce odorous sulfur compounds. Stopping removes the smoke source and the associated risk factor.
Risks and caveats: No harms from the practice itself are reported in the sources consulted. Nicotine withdrawal is a general clinical consideration and cessation support is available through clinicians. No appearance-specific trials were found.
deepLead:
Quitting smoking and vaping for breath and oral appearance refers to the practice of stopping tobacco and nicotine use in order to reduce smoke odour on the breath and to protect the gums. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and grooming circles as a low-cost lifestyle change, alongside oral hygiene and dental care.
Reference sources link smoking to periodontal (gum) disease, which is described as the second most common cause of oral malodour (bad breath) after bacterial coating on the tongue . Smoking is also described as arguably the most important environmental risk factor for periodontitis, with smokers showing more bone loss, attachment loss and tooth loss than non-smokers . The same sources state that quitting improves periodontal health .
No trials specific to appearance outcomes of quitting were identified for this article, and the evidence on vaping and gum health is not covered in the reference material consulted.

name: Retainer and mouthguard cleaning

angle.text: Grooming-minded users clean retainers and mouthguards to avoid bacterial buildup and odour. The idea is plausible by analogy with denture hygiene, with little direct study.

summary: Routine cleaning of retainers and mouthguards to limit bacterial buildup and odour; plausible by analogy to dentures, but little direct study.
note: Sources found cover related appliances (dentures), not retainers directly.
currentQuick:
Cleaning retainers and mouthguards is a hygiene habit meant to prevent bacterial buildup and odour.
Reference sources describe bacteria and yeast building up on porous acrylic dentures, a related appliance, but no studies specific to retainers or mouthguards were found.
How it works: Appliances worn in the mouth can collect biofilm on their surfaces; cleaning removes it. Porous plastic is described as especially able to hold microbes.
Risks and caveats: No harms from cleaning are reported in the sources consulted. Manufacturers and dentists give product-specific care guidance.
deepLead:
Retainer and mouthguard cleaning refers to routine hygiene for removable oral appliances such as orthodontic retainers, sports mouthguards and night guards. In grooming-oriented communities it is mentioned as a way to avoid bacterial buildup and odour.
Reference material on closely related appliances notes that porous acrylic dentures can harbour bacteria and yeast and cause odour when not cleaned well . Wikipedia's mouthguard article describes how occlusal splints are typically made of heat-cured acrylic or softer materials but does not discuss cleaning .
No studies specific to retainer or mouthguard cleaning were identified for this article, so the entry is short.

name: Laser iris depigmentation (Stroma laser)

angle.text: Hardmaxxing communities discuss it as a way to lighten brown eyes without an implant. Reference summaries say it is not approved for cosmetic use and no trials were found.

summary: A laser procedure meant to lighten iris color; unapproved for cosmetic use per reference summaries, with glaucoma and cataract listed as risks and no trials found.
note: Reference summaries list glaucoma, cataract and unpredictable color results as risks.
currentQuick:
Laser iris depigmentation aims to lighten eye color by using a laser to reduce pigment in the iris.
No clinical trials of the cosmetic procedure were found, and a reference summary states it is not FDA approved for cosmetic use.
How it works: Eye color is determined by iris melanin; the procedure is meant to remove some of that pigment so the eye looks lighter.
Risks and caveats: Listed risks include raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, cataracts and unpredictable color outcomes. Ophthalmologists criticize cosmetic alteration of healthy eyes because of potential vision loss.
deepLead:
Laser iris depigmentation is a procedure, promoted for cosmetic eye color change, in which a laser is directed at the iris to reduce its melanin pigment and lighten the eye, typically from brown toward a lighter shade. It is discussed in hardmaxxing communities as a way to change eye color without an implant.
A Grokipedia summary of eye color change methods lists risks of laser depigmentation including raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, cataracts and unpredictable color results, and states that the US FDA has not approved it for cosmetic use . Eye color is described as determined by iris melanin, which is why pigment-targeting methods have been proposed .
No clinical trials of the cosmetic procedure were found among the sources reviewed.

name: NewColorIris cosmetic implants

chain: Silicone iris placed in the eye
angle.text: These implants were placed in healthy eyes to change eye colour, with the new colour visible once in place. Published case series report serious complications, and the brand is described as no longer in use.

summary: Silicone iris implants placed in healthy eyes to change color; published case series report glaucoma, corneal damage and vision loss, and the brand is described as no longer in use.
note: Case reports describe serious complications, often needing explantation.
currentQuick:
NewColorIris implants are colored silicone discs surgically placed in healthy eyes to change eye color.
Published case series report serious complications such as raised eye pressure, glaucoma and corneal damage. Ophthalmologists have criticized the use of artificial irises in healthy eyes.
How it works: A foldable silicone implant sits in front of the natural iris and shows through the cornea in the chosen color.
Risks and caveats: Reported harms include elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, corneal decompensation, inflammation and vision loss, with removal often required. One paper states NewColorIris implants are no longer in use. Evidence is limited to case reports.
deepLead:
NewColorIris is a brand of foldable silicone artificial iris implants that were surgically placed in the anterior chamber of healthy eyes to change eye color for cosmetic reasons. Artificial irises are marketed as an alternative to cosmetic contact lenses, and ophthalmologists have criticized implanting them in healthy eyes because of the risk of vision loss .
Published case reports and series describe serious complications after cosmetic implantation, including raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, corneal decompensation, inflammation and cataract, often requiring removal . A paper on a newer implant, BrightOcular, states that NewColorIris implants have a record of high ocular morbidity and are no longer in use .
The evidence consists of case reports and case series rather than controlled trials.

name: Hypnosis for eye color change

angle.text: Fringe corners of appearance culture claim hypnosis or suggestion recordings can alter iris colour. No studies have tested it, and reference sources report no evidence that hypnosis changes physical traits.

summary: The claim that hypnosis can change iris color; no studies have tested it and reference sources report no evidence hypnosis alters physical traits.
note: Untested; money spent on courses or recordings is the main reported cost.
currentQuick:
Some fringe sources claim hypnosis or suggestion can change eye color.
No studies have tested this, and general references on hypnosis report no evidence that it alters physical characteristics.
How it works: Proponents say suggestion influences the body. Research on hypnosis describes effects on perception and involuntary responses, not on iris pigment.
Risks and caveats: No direct physical harms are documented. Unproven claims may lead people to delay or substitute other options.
deepLead:
Hypnosis for eye color change is a claim, found in fringe corners of appearance culture, that hypnosis, self-hypnosis or suggestion recordings can alter the color of a person's irises.
Wikipedia describes hypnosis as a state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility and reports no evidence that it alters physical characteristics such as body structure or appearance . Research cited there shows suggestion can affect sensation, perception and some involuntary responses, and that brain imaging changes under suggestion may reflect stronger imagination rather than real perceptual change .
No published studies were found that tested hypnosis for changing eye color.

name: Honey drops in eyes

angle.text: A folk claim in eye-colour discussions says diluted honey lightens the iris. It is untested and not an established cosmetic procedure, and ophthalmologists advise against related lightening drops.

summary: A folk claim that honey in the eyes lightens iris color; untested, and related lightening drops are advised against by ophthalmologists.
note: Putting non-sterile substances in the eye carries general infection risk.
currentQuick:
Some folk sources say honey drops can lighten eye color.
No studies have tested this, and general references describe eye color as fixed by iris pigment.
How it works: Proponents claim a gradual bleaching effect. No mechanism has been shown in research.
Risks and caveats: Non-sterile substances in the eye are generally associated with irritation and infection; the AAO has advised against lightening drops in general.
deepLead:
Honey drops in eyes is a folk claim that putting diluted honey in the eyes can lighten the iris color. It appears in fringe eye-color discussions and is not an established cosmetic procedure.
Wikipedia's honey article contains little on eye use; it states honey is generally considered ineffective for allergic conjunctivitis . No published studies were found testing honey drops for changing eye color.
General reference sources describe eye color as set by iris pigmentation, and note that over-the-counter lightening drops of other kinds lack proven effectiveness, with the American Academy of Ophthalmology advising against them in 2024 .

name: Eye color meditation / visualization

angle.text: Practitioners in wellness and self-transformation circles meditate or visualize a different color in the hope of changing their iris shade, as a non-invasive alternative to colored lenses or surgery. The idea rests on belief and anecdote; no study has tested it.

summary: Trying to change iris color by meditating or picturing a new shade; no study has tested it and iris color is set by melanin and genes.
note: No published human studies; physical methods of changing eye color carry documented risks and are a separate topic.
currentQuick:
Eye color meditation is the idea that focused visualization or affirmation can gradually change the color of your irises. It is shared in wellness and self-improvement spaces as a free, non-invasive option.
Reference works describe iris color as determined by melanin and genetics, and do not list meditation among the known influences. No clinical study has tested the practice.
How it works: Practitioners sit and imagine a target eye color, often with affirmations, over an extended period. No physiological mechanism linking this to iris melanin has been described in published research; known natural changes occur through development, hormones, medications or disease.
Risks and caveats: The practice itself is non-invasive and no direct harms have been reported. Ophthalmology bodies warn about other eye-color-changing products and procedures, and sudden real changes in eye color can accompany medical conditions.
deepLead:
Eye color meditation or visualization is a practice in which people try to change the color of their irises by meditating, affirming or mentally picturing a different color. It circulates in wellness and self-transformation circles and in some appearance-focused online communities as a non-invasive alternative to cosmetic lenses or surgical procedures.
Reference works on eye color describe it as determined mainly by the amount and distribution of melanin in the iris, with the HERC2-OCA2 region on chromosome 15 and several other genes contributing . Neither of the encyclopedia articles consulted mentions meditation or visualization as a recognized influence on iris color , and no published clinical study has tested the practice.

name: Eye color diet

angle.text: Wellness and appearance forums promote foods, hydration habits and supplements as ways to lighten the iris without lenses or procedures. The link to iris pigment is a belief; no trial has tested diet for eye color.

summary: Food and supplement routines said to lighten the eyes; iris color is set by melanin and genes and no trial has tested diet.
note: No published human studies; no recognized dietary influence on iris pigment.
currentQuick:
The eye color diet is the claim that eating or avoiding certain things can lighten or change your iris color. It is passed around in wellness and appearance communities as a no-procedure route.
Encyclopedia sources attribute iris color to melanin and genes and do not list diet as an influence. No clinical study has tested the idea.
How it works: Proponents generally propose that diet or supplements reduce iris melanin or brighten the eyes, but no pathway from food to iris pigment has been described in published research. Natural color shifts are linked to development, hormones, medications and disease.
Risks and caveats: Dietary approaches have no reported direct eye harms in the sources reviewed, though restrictive diets carry their own considerations. Ophthalmology bodies warn against eye-color-changing procedures and drops, and sudden real color change can signal a medical condition.
deepLead:
The eye color diet refers to claims that particular foods, supplements, hydration habits or eating patterns can lighten or otherwise change the color of the iris. It appears in wellness content and appearance-focused online discussion as a way to alter eye color without lenses or procedures.
Reference works describe iris color as set mainly by melanin in the iris and by genes such as OCA2 and HERC2 . Neither article consulted lists diet as a recognized influence on iris pigmentation, and Grokipedia's article on eye color states that drinking water or hydration does not change iris pigmentation, though hydration may improve the overall look of the eyes . No published clinical study has tested a diet for changing iris color.

name: Limbal ring contact lenses

angle.text: Users wear these cosmetic lenses to add a dark outer iris ring, which gives eyes a more defined, striking look the moment they are in. Circle designs also make the iris appear larger. Attractiveness studies exist for natural limbal rings, not for the lenses.

summary: Tinted contacts that add a dark rim to the iris for a younger, more striking look; the ring itself has attractiveness studies, the lenses do not.
note: Prescription required in the US; cosmetic lenses carry infection and corneal ulcer risks.
currentQuick:
Limbal ring contact lenses are cosmetic soft lenses with a dark band at the iris edge, designed to mimic the dark ring seen in young eyes. Some are ring-only; larger circle lenses also make the iris look wider.
Studies on natural limbal rings found faces with them rated more attractive or healthier-looking, but no study has tested the lenses themselves.
How it works: The lens carries a printed dark annulus that sits over the iris-sclera border, increasing apparent contrast. The effect lasts only while the lenses are worn.
Risks and caveats: Cosmetic lenses carry the usual risks of irritation, infection and corneal ulcers, particularly with poor hygiene or overnight wear. In the US they are regulated medical devices requiring a prescription, even with zero power.
deepLead:
Limbal ring contact lenses are cosmetic soft lenses printed with a dark band at the outer edge of the iris, imitating a prominent limbal ring. Some designs only darken the iris border, while others (often called circle lenses) extend the dark rim outward so the iris appears larger .
Interest among looksmaxxing communities follows the idea that a dark limbal ring makes the eyes look younger, healthier and more striking. Wikipedia's limbal ring article reports that two published studies found observers rating faces with limbal rings as more attractive or health-signalling , but no study has specifically tested limbal ring lenses. Like other contact lenses, cosmetic lenses carry risks of irritation and infection, and in the United States they are regulated as medical devices requiring a prescription, including zero-power versions .

name: Limbal ring theory

angle.text: Forum posters treat a prominent limbal ring as a key eye feature that signals youth and health, and discuss ways to gain or imitate one, including lenses. Small perception studies support the attractiveness link; the claim about body sulfur setting ring darkness is anecdotal.

summary: The idea that a dark ring around the iris signals youth and health; small perception studies support it, forums treat it as a major eye feature.
note: Evidence is limited to a few observer-rating studies; claims about boosting the ring are untested.
currentQuick:
The limbal ring is the dark band at the edge of the iris. Limbal ring theory says a prominent ring reads as youthful and healthy, and makes eyes more attractive.
A 2011 study found faces with a darker ring were rated more attractive, and a 2018 study found women read men's rings as a health cue in short-term mating contexts. The research base is small.
How it works: The ring arises from the optics of the cornea-sclera junction plus pigment in the peripheral iris in some people. It is most visible in youth and fades with age and some eye conditions. Online, people discuss ways to make it appear darker, mainly cosmetic lenses.
Risks and caveats: The ring itself is a natural feature with no associated risk. Methods people use to imitate it, such as cosmetic contact lenses, carry the usual lens risks and in the US require a prescription.
deepLead:
Limbal ring theory is the idea, common in looksmaxxing and attractiveness discussions, that the dark ring around the iris signals youth and health, and that a prominent ring therefore makes a face more attractive. The limbal ring is the darker band visible where the iris meets the white of the eye (the sclera), at the corneal limbus .
Anatomical references describe the ring as arising largely from the optics of the cornea-sclera junction, with pigment contributions in some people. It is typically most prominent in childhood and young adulthood and tends to fade with age and with some eye conditions . Two published studies, in 2011 and 2018, reported that observers rated faces with limbal rings as more attractive or as health cues . Looksmaxxing forums discuss the ring as a feature that makes eyes more striking and ask how it might be darkened or thickened .

name: Brimonidine drops (Lumify)

angle.text: Users apply low-dose over-the-counter brimonidine drops to make the whites of the eyes look clearer for a few hours. Its cleared use is temporary redness relief; the cosmetic whitening use is off its labeled purpose and untested as a beauty practice.

summary: Low-dose OTC brimonidine drops that shrink eye-surface vessels for whiter-looking sclera; FDA-cleared for redness, untested as a cosmetic.
note: Labeled for short-term redness relief only; forum users discuss frequent use and alternating with other drops, which no study has examined.
currentQuick:
Lumify is a low-dose brimonidine eye drop sold over the counter in the US for temporary relief of eye redness. In looksmaxxing circles it is used for a whiter sclera and a brighter eye look.
The redness-relief use is FDA-approved; use as a cosmetic enhancer, including claims about eye color, has not been studied.
How it works: Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that constricts blood vessels on the eye surface, reducing visible redness. Onset is reported at about a minute with effect lasting up to several hours.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include itching, redness, dry mouth and rarer allergic reactions. Rebound redness has been described with the brimonidine rosacea gel; its extent with Lumify is not characterized in the sources reviewed. Labeling says it is for minor irritation, not glaucoma or serious eye conditions.
deepLead:
Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used in prescription eye drops to lower eye pressure in glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and as a topical gel that reduces facial redness in rosacea . At a low concentration of 0.025 percent it is sold over the counter as Lumify, made by Bausch + Lomb, for temporary relief of eye redness from minor irritations .
In looksmaxxing communities Lumify is discussed as a way to whiten the sclera by shrinking visible blood vessels, and some users say it also makes lighter irises look different in color. Forum posts also show users asking how often it can safely be used and discussing alternating it with other redness drops. Regulatory labeling describes it as a short-term redness reliever and the product is not intended for glaucoma or other serious eye conditions . No published trial has examined it specifically as an appearance enhancer; registered trials of Lumify have studied redness comparisons, eyelid position and related questions.

name: Tetrahydrozoline drops (Visine)

angle.text: People use these over-the-counter drops for fast whitening of the sclera before photos or events. The visible redness reduction is quick; it is labeled for minor irritation redness, and its repeated cosmetic use has been studied mainly for rebound redness.

summary: OTC redness drops (0.05% tetrahydrozoline) that whiten the sclera fast, with well-known rebound redness on repeated use.
note: Rebound redness with prolonged use; oral ingestion is dangerous, especially for children.
currentQuick:
Visine-type drops contain tetrahydrozoline, a vasoconstrictor that shrinks surface blood vessels in the eye to reduce redness. Looksmaxxers use them for whiter sclera.
The redness-relief effect is established and the product is sold over the counter for short-term use. Reference sources describe rebound redness after prolonged use, and no study has examined it as a cosmetic treatment.
How it works: Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, constricting vessels on the eye surface. Effects start within minutes and its half-life is about 6 hours.
Risks and caveats: Prolonged use can lead to tolerance and rebound redness, and eye drops may cause blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils. Swallowing the product can cause serious poisoning, especially in children, with no antidote. Labels advise seeing a doctor for persistent redness and removing contact lenses first.
deepLead:
Tetrahydrozoline (also spelled tetryzoline) is an over-the-counter vasoconstrictor used in eye drops and nasal sprays. The best-known redness-relief eye drop containing it is Visine, which contains 0.05 percent tetrahydrozoline hydrochloride and is sold to temporarily relieve eye redness from minor irritations .
In looksmaxxing communities such drops are discussed as a quick way to whiten the sclera and brighten the eyes. Reference sources note that tetrahydrozoline is not meant for prolonged use because tolerance can develop and stopping it can cause rebound redness , and forum users themselves frequently mention rebound as a drawback and compare it unfavorably with brimonidine-based drops . Accidental or deliberate oral ingestion can cause serious poisoning, particularly in children .

name: Artificial tears

angle.text: Appearance communities use lubricating drops as basic eye comfort care, since dry and irritated eyes tend to look redder and more tired. They are studied for dry eye and lens comfort, not as a whitening product.

summary: Over-the-counter lubricating eye drops for dry, irritated eyes: standard first-line comfort care, not a whitening or redness fix.
note: Redness-relief drops containing vasoconstrictors such as tetrahydrozoline are a different product class; a 2023 contamination recall of some brands was linked to serious infections.
currentQuick:
Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments sold mostly without prescription. They are used for dry eye and for irritation from screens, wind, contact lenses or surgery, and in appearance circles they are discussed as a way to keep the eye surface comfortable and less irritated-looking.
They come with or without preservatives, in thin liquid or thicker gel forms. Reviews and guidance describe them as the usual first step for dry eye, though no single formulation has been shown to be best.
How it works: They supplement and stabilise the tear film that coats the eye, using water, salts and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose or hyaluronic acid. They do not contain the living components of natural tears and do not treat the underlying cause of dryness.
Risks and caveats: Temporary blurred vision is the most common effect, especially with gels and ointments. Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride can irritate the eye surface with frequent use, which is why preservative-free vials are recommended for heavy use. In 2023 a recall of certain brands followed bacterial contamination linked to eye infections, vision loss and a death. Drops marketed to remove redness contain different active ingredients.
deepLead:
Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments that are designed to relieve dryness and irritation of the ocular surface. They are sold mostly over the counter and are used mainly for dry eye disease, for contact lens comfort and during or after some eye procedures .
Formulations are built from water, electrolytes and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, polyvinyl alcohol, hypromellose, hydroxypropyl cellulose or hyaluronic acid. They are made with or without preservatives, and as thin drops for daytime or thicker gels and ointments for longer-lasting but vision-blurring effect .
Published reviews have found no clear single best formulation, and many trials of individual products are small or open-label . In looksmaxxing and appearance contexts artificial tears are sometimes discussed as supportive eye-surface care, distinct from whitening drops or surgical options.

name: Scleral whitening / conjunctivectomy

angle.text: This elective surgery, sold under names like I-BRITE, aims at a lasting whiter look by treating the conjunctival tissue and vessels. The change is visible after healing; published reports are mostly case reports of late complications.

summary: Elective surgery that removes or cauterises conjunctival tissue to make the whites of the eyes look whiter; published reports are limited to case reports of late complications.
note: Case reports describe regrowth of redness and severe scleral necrosis years after the procedure.
currentQuick:
Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or conjunctivectomy, is an elective operation aimed at making the visible white of the eye look whiter by removing or treating the surface tissue that carries blood vessels. One branded version is called I-BRITE.
The literature on the cosmetic procedure is thin. The published material found consists mainly of individual case reports describing late problems and a case where a patient used painted contact lenses to mask returning redness.
How it works: As described in the case literature, the procedure involves dissecting the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, applying cautery and using mitomycin C, an agent that limits tissue regrowth. The goal is to prevent visible blood vessels and redness from returning.
Risks and caveats: A case report describes severe pain, scleral inflammation and necrosis in both eyes nine years after the procedure, treated with immunosuppressive therapy. Another report describes recurrent conjunctival redness five years afterward. No controlled trials of the cosmetic procedure were found.
deepLead:
Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or cosmetic conjunctivectomy, is an elective procedure intended to make the white of the eye appear whiter by removing or treating the conjunctival tissue and its blood vessels. One commercially named version is I-BRITE .
According to published case descriptions, the operation involves dissection of the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, cautery and application of mitomycin C . Mitomycin C is an antiproliferative drug used in several eye surgeries.
No controlled studies of the cosmetic procedure were identified. The published literature consists of case reports describing late complications, including surgically induced scleral necrosis, and the recurrence of conjunctival redness .

name: Pinguecula / pterygium removal

angle.text: Some people have yellowish or pinkish growths on the white of the eye removed to even out its look, though surgery is mainly done for medical reasons. The visible clearing of the growth is the result itself.

summary: Surgery to remove the yellowish or pinkish conjunctival growths of pinguecula and pterygium, done mainly for medical reasons and sometimes for looks.
note: Pterygium can recur after surgery, so technique and follow-up matter in the published studies.
currentQuick:
A pinguecula is a yellowish bump on the white of the eye, and a pterygium is a related fleshy, often pink growth that extends onto the cornea. Both are linked to long-term sun and dust exposure. Removal is a recognised eye operation, mostly for vision, irritation or contact lens problems, and some people seek it for cosmetic reasons.
The surgical literature is large for pterygium and focuses on recurrence rates, techniques and effects on corneal shape. Pinguecula removal has far less published research.
How it works: The growth is surgically excised. Modern techniques usually cover the bare area with tissue, most often a conjunctival autograft from the same eye, held with sutures or tissue glue, to reduce regrowth. Other approaches in the literature include amniotic membrane, mitomycin C and, historically, beta irradiation.
Risks and caveats: Recurrence is the main reported problem, with rates varying widely by technique and population; an encyclopedic summary says about half of cases recur, while grafting studies report lower figures. Other documented issues include corneal astigmatism changes and complications of adjunct treatments such as radiation.
deepLead:
A pinguecula is a yellowish raised area of the conjunctiva, and a pterygium is a related triangular growth that extends from the conjunctiva onto the cornea. Both are associated with ultraviolet light and dust exposure; a pterygium is sometimes called surfer's eye .
Removal is typically considered when a pterygium affects vision through astigmatism or scarring, causes persistent irritation or contact lens intolerance, or is cosmetically bothersome. Many cases need no surgery, and artificial tears are commonly used for irritation .
The surgical literature has examined techniques such as bare sclera excision, conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, mitomycin C and radiation, with recurrence as the central outcome .

name: Antihistamine eye drops

angle.text: Users with allergic eyes use these drops to reduce itching, redness and lid swelling, which can make the eyes look clearer. They are studied for allergic conjunctivitis; appearance for non-allergic eyes is untested.

summary: Allergy eye drops such as olopatadine and ketotifen that treat itchy, red allergic eyes; some brands pair an antihistamine with a redness-reliever.
note: Redness only counts as allergic if allergy is the cause; combination products with a vasoconstrictor such as naphazoline are a separate category.
currentQuick:
Antihistamine eye drops treat the itching, redness and watering caused by allergic conjunctivitis. Common active ingredients include olopatadine and ketotifen, which are available without prescription in some countries, and combination products that add a vasoconstrictor such as naphazoline.
In appearance discussions they come up as a way to reduce allergy-related red eyes. Studies in the sources compare initial comfort of different brands and the evidence base is about allergic eye symptoms, not general whitening.
How it works: Antihistamines block histamine receptors on the eye surface, and several drops (olopatadine, ketotifen) also stabilise mast cells, the cells that release histamine. Naphazoline-containing combinations additionally narrow surface blood vessels to reduce visible redness.
Risks and caveats: Drops commonly cause burning or stinging on instillation, and comfort differs between products. Eye care guidance generally treats vasoconstrictor-containing products as unsuitable for long continuous use, since prolonged use can worsen redness. A survey of Australian practitioners found variation in how ocular allergy is managed.
deepLead:
Antihistamine eye drops are topical medicines for allergic conjunctivitis, a reaction to allergens such as pollen, animal dander, dust mites or cosmetics that causes itching, redness, tearing and eyelid swelling .
Many contemporary products have dual activity, blocking histamine receptors and stabilising mast cells. Olopatadine and ketotifen are named examples, and some are sold over the counter . Other products combine an antihistamine such as pheniramine with the vasoconstrictor naphazoline .
Published comparisons in the sources address ocular comfort at instillation rather than cosmetic outcomes .
